definition: A binary digit: the smallest unit of information, holding one of two values written 0 and 1. Every number, character and instruction in a computer is stored as a pattern of bits.
example: The 8 bits 01000001 can mean the number 65 or the letter A, depending on how a program reads them.

definition: A group of bits handled as a unit; today almost always 8 bits, and the smallest piece of memory that has its own address on common processors. Some historical machines and some DSPs use other sizes.
example: One byte can hold 256 different values, 0 to 255.

definition: Exactly 8 bits. Network and file-format standards say octet rather than byte because, historically, a byte was not always 8 bits.
example: An IPv4 address is four octets, such as 192.168.1.10.

definition: Four bits, half a byte. One nibble is exactly one hexadecimal digit.
example: The byte 0xB5 has high nibble B (1011) and low nibble 5 (0101).

definition: The natural unit of data a processor works with, usually the width of its general-purpose registers. Its size depends on the architecture and on the document: x86 manuals call 16 bits a WORD, ARM calls 32 bits a word, and a 64-bit CPU has 64-bit registers.
example: On a 64-bit processor, adding two 64-bit integers takes one instruction because 64 bits is its word size.

definition: x86 names for data sizes: a WORD is 16 bits, a DWORD (double word) 32 bits and a QWORD (quad word) 64 bits. The names date from the 16-bit Intel 8086 and were kept on 32- and 64-bit chips.
example: A Windows API parameter of type DWORD is a 32-bit unsigned integer, even in a 64-bit program.

definition: In ARM terminology, a 16-bit quantity: half of ARM's 32-bit word.
example: ARM's LDRH instruction loads a halfword (2 bytes) from memory.

definition: Twice a word. In ARM terminology a doubleword is 64 bits; in x86 terminology a doubleword (DWORD) is 32 bits, because there a word is 16 bits.
example: An ARM doubleword holds one 64-bit integer.

definition: The number of different digits a positional number system uses, which is also how much each position is worth relative to the one to its right. Decimal has radix 10, binary 2, octal 8 and hexadecimal 16.
example: In radix 16, the number 10 means sixteen.

definition: A way of writing numbers in which a digit's value depends on its position: each position is worth the base raised to the position number. Decimal, binary and hexadecimal are all positional.
example: In 472, the 4 is worth 400 because it sits in the hundreds position.

definition: The base-2 number system, which uses only the digits 0 and 1; each position is worth twice the one to its right (1, 2, 4, 8...). Computers use it because two states are easy to store and switch reliably.
example: Binary 1011 is 8 + 2 + 1 = 11 in decimal.

definition: The everyday base-10 number system, with digits 0 to 9; each position is worth ten times the one to its right.
example: Decimal 181 is 1 hundred, 8 tens and 1 one.

definition: The base-16 number system, using digits 0 to 9 and then A to F for ten to fifteen. One hex digit is exactly four bits, so programmers use it as a compact way to write binary; in C and Python it is written with a 0x prefix.
example: 0xFF is 255, the largest value of one byte.

definition: The base-8 number system, using digits 0 to 7. One octal digit is exactly three bits; today it is mostly seen in Unix file permissions. Python writes it with a 0o prefix, while C treats a leading 0 as octal.
example: Octal 755 is binary 111 101 101.

definition: The rightmost bit of a binary number, worth 1 (2 to the power 0). Whether it is 1 tells you whether the number is odd.
example: The LSB of 181 (10110101) is 1, so 181 is odd.

definition: The leftmost bit of a binary number, the one with the largest weight. In a signed two's complement number it is the sign bit.
example: In an 8-bit value the MSB is bit 7, worth 128 unsigned or −128 signed.

definition: The byte of a multi-byte value that holds its lowest-weighted 8 bits. Little-endian machines store it at the lowest address.
example: In 0x12345678 the least significant byte is 0x78.

definition: The byte of a multi-byte value that holds its highest-weighted 8 bits. Big-endian machines and network byte order put it first.
example: In 0x12345678 the most significant byte is 0x12.

definition: A number made by multiplying 2 by itself some number of times: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32... In binary a power of two has exactly one 1-bit, which makes powers of two natural sizes for memory, tables and alignment.
example: 1,024 is 2 to the power 10, so it is binary 1 followed by ten 0s.

definition: Repeated multiplication: b to the power n, written b^n, means n copies of b multiplied together. Any non-zero number to the power 0 is 1, and a negative power means 1 divided by the positive power.
The capital Greek letter sigma, Σ, means 'add up': add the expression after it once for each value of its counting variable.
example: Σ d_i × 2^i over the bits 101 gives 4 + 0 + 1 = 5.

definition: Writing a number as a few digits times a power of ten, such as 6.02 × 10^3 for 6,020. Programming languages write the power with an e, so 1.19e−7 means 1.19 × 10^−7 and 3.4e38 means 3.4 × 10^38.
example: The mass of the Sun is about 2 × 10^30 kg, a 2 followed by 30 zeros.

definition: The whole-number result of a division, ignoring what is left over (the remainder).
example: 181 ÷ 2 has quotient 90 and remainder 1.

definition: What is left over when one whole number is divided by another and only the whole-number quotient is kept. Repeated division by a base, keeping the remainders, converts a number into that base.
example: 200 ÷ 16 is 12 with remainder 8.

definition: In a division a ÷ b, a is the dividend (the number being divided) and b is the divisor (the number divided by). In C and Java the sign of a remainder follows the dividend.
example: In −17 % 5 the dividend is −17, so Java's result is −2.

definition: Arithmetic that wraps around after reaching a fixed number, the modulus, like a clock wrapping from 12 back to 1. Two numbers are equal modulo m when they differ by a whole multiple of m. Fixed-width n-bit integer arithmetic is arithmetic modulo 2 to the power n.
example: 255 + 1 is 0 modulo 256, which is why an 8-bit counter wraps to 0.

definition: The symbol ≡ means two numbers are equal in modular arithmetic: a ≡ b (mod m) says a and b leave the same remainder when divided by m.
example: −5 ≡ 251 (mod 256), so −5 and 251 are the same 8-bit pattern.

definition: Rounding down to the nearest whole number, towards negative infinity, written ⌊x⌋. So ⌊2.7⌋ = 2 and ⌊−2.5⌋ = −3. An arithmetic right shift divides by a power of two with floor rounding.
Rounding up to the nearest whole number, written ⌈x⌉. So ⌈9.97⌉ = 10. It answers questions like 'how many bits or bytes are needed at minimum'.
example: Storing 1,000 values needs ⌈log₂ 1000⌉ = 10 bits.

definition: Dropping the fractional part of a number, so the result moves towards zero: 2.7 becomes 2 and −2.7 becomes −2. C99 and later define integer division this way.
example: In C, −17 / 2 is −8, because −8.5 is truncated towards zero.

definition: The inverse of raising to a power: log base 2 of x is the power you must raise 2 to in order to get x. It tells you how many bits are needed to count up to x.
example: log₂(1,024) = 10, because 2 to the power 10 is 1,024.

definition: A number with digits after the binary point, where the positions are worth 1/2, 1/4, 1/8 and so on. Only fractions whose reduced denominator is a power of two have a finite binary form.
The bottom number of a fraction, the number of equal parts the whole is split into; the top number is the numerator.
example: In 3/8 the denominator is 8.

definition: A fraction written so that its top and bottom share no common factor other than 1.
example: 6/16 in lowest terms is 3/8.

definition: A prime number (one divisible only by 1 and itself, such as 2, 3, 5 or 7) that divides a given number exactly. 10 has prime factors 2 and 5.
example: The 5 in 10 = 2 × 5 is why 1/10 never ends in binary.

definition: Three groups of three bits (read, write, execute) controlling what a file's owner, its group and everyone else may do with it. Each group is usually written as one octal digit with r = 4, w = 2 and x = 1.
example: Mode 640 means owner rw-, group r--, others ---.

definition: The Unix command (and system call) that changes a file's permission bits, often given as three octal digits.
example: chmod 755 script.sh lets everyone read and run the script but only the owner change it.

definition: A per-process set of permission bits that are removed from the mode of every new file the process creates.
example: With umask 022, open(..., 0666) creates a file with mode 0644.

definition: A number written directly in source code. A prefix selects the base: 0x for hexadecimal, 0b for binary, 0o for octal in Python, and in C a bare leading 0 for octal.
example: In C, 010 is the integer literal eight, not ten.

definition: The Python exception raised when source code breaks the language's grammar, so the program will not run at all.
example: Python 3 raises SyntaxError for 010 and requires 0o10.

definition: A compiled systems programming language from the early 1970s, standardised by ISO, used for operating systems, embedded firmware and performance-critical code. Its rules on integer sizes, overflow and memory layout are central to this module.
example: The Linux kernel is written mainly in C.

definition: The 1999 revision of the ISO C standard. Among other changes it fixed integer division to round towards zero and added fixed-width types such as uint32_t.
example: Under C99, −7 / 2 is guaranteed to be −3.

definition: The 2024-published revision of the ISO C standard (ISO/IEC 9899:2024). It requires two's complement signed integers, standardises binary literals (0b...) and adds checked-arithmetic functions such as ckd_add.
example: In C23, int x = 0b1010; is standard code.

definition: A programming language derived from C, adding classes, templates and much more. C++20 requires two's complement signed integers; C++17 added hardware_destructive_interference_size.
example: Most game engines are written in C++.

definition: The GNU Compiler Collection, a widely used free compiler for C, C++ and other languages, standard on most Linux systems.
example: gcc -O2 -fwrapv prog.c compiles with optimisation and wrapping signed arithmetic.

definition: A C, C++ and Objective-C compiler front end built on the LLVM project; the default compiler on macOS and largely compatible with GCC's options.
example: clang -fsanitize=undefined enables UBSan checks.

definition: Microsoft Visual C++, Microsoft's C and C++ compiler for Windows.
example: MSVC accepts #pragma pack(1) to remove struct padding.

definition: The C standard library function that prints formatted text. Conversion specifiers choose the format: %d for signed decimal, %x for hexadecimal, %o for octal, %zu for size_t.
example: printf("%x", 181u) prints b5.

definition: A C constant giving the number of bits in a byte (a char). The C standard only requires it to be at least 8; POSIX requires exactly 8.
example: On ordinary PCs and phones, CHAR_BIT is 8.

definition: Decimal multiplier prefixes from the International System of Units: kilo (k) = 1,000, mega (M) = 10^6, giga (G) = 10^9, tera (T) = 10^12. Drive makers use them for capacity.
example: A 2 TB drive holds 2 × 10^12 bytes.

definition: Prefixes standardised by the IEC (International Electrotechnical Commission) for powers of 1,024: kibi (Ki) = 2^10, mebi (Mi) = 2^20, gibi (Gi) = 2^30, tebi (Ti) = 2^40. They exist because kilo, mega and giga officially mean powers of 1,000.
example: 1 GiB = 1,073,741,824 bytes, about 7.4% more than 1 GB.

definition: 1,000 bytes under the SI meaning of kilo. KB in capitals is often used informally, and sometimes to mean 1,024 bytes, which is exactly the ambiguity the KiB unit removes.
example: A 50 kB image file is 50,000 bytes.

definition: One million (10^6) bytes in SI usage. Some software uses MB for 1,048,576 bytes, properly called a mebibyte (MiB).
example: Ten million 24-byte structs take 240 MB.

definition: 10^9 (a thousand million) bytes in SI usage. Some operating systems display GB when they really mean gibibytes (GiB).
example: A 1 TB drive may show as about 931 GB, which is really 931 GiB.

definition: 10^12 (a million million) bytes, the SI unit drive makers use for capacity.
example: A 2 TB drive holds 2,000,000,000,000 bytes.

definition: 1,024 (2^10) bytes, the IEC binary unit.
example: A 4 KiB memory page is 4,096 bytes.
8 MiB is 8,388,608 bytes.
A 2 TB drive holds about 1,862.6 GiB.
1 TB is about 0.9095 TiB.

definition: A 48-bit hardware address that identifies a network interface on a local network, usually written as six hex bytes.
example: A MAC address looks like 3C:22:FB:8A:01:7E.

definition: A fixed-size number computed from data by a hash function, used to look items up quickly or to check data has not changed. Hashes are usually printed in hexadecimal.
example: A SHA-256 hash is 256 bits, shown as 64 hex digits.

definition: A data structure that stores items in an array of buckets, choosing each item's bucket from its hash value, so lookups take about the same time however many items there are.
example: Java's HashMap keeps its bucket count a power of two so it can pick a bucket with a mask.

definition: A listing of the raw bytes in a region of memory or a file, usually shown in hexadecimal; used for debugging and reverse engineering.
example: A hex dump of a little-endian 0x12345678 shows 78 56 34 12.

definition: A processor specialised for signal-processing arithmetic such as filtering audio. Some DSPs cannot address single 8-bit bytes, so their C char is 16 or 32 bits.
example: Some Texas Instruments C2000 DSPs have a 16-bit char.

definition: A small, very fast storage slot inside the processor that instructions read and write directly. The width of the general-purpose registers is what makes a CPU '32-bit' or '64-bit'.
example: x86-64 has sixteen 64-bit general-purpose registers, such as RAX.

definition: An address as a program sees it. Hardware and the operating system translate it to a physical address; current 64-bit CPUs typically implement only 48 or 57 bits of virtual address.
example: On x86-64 with 4-level paging, user pointers use the low 47 bits.

definition: The actual location in memory hardware that a virtual address is translated to. Its width depends on the processor and need not match the virtual address width.
example: A CPU may support 52-bit physical addresses but 48-bit virtual ones.

definition: Intel's 16-bit microprocessor from 1978, the ancestor of the x86 family; its 16-bit word is why x86 still calls 16 bits a WORD.
example: Today's x86-64 chips can still run 8086 instructions in their oldest mode.

definition: Intel's family of instruction set architectures descended from the 8086. x86-64 (also AMD64 or x64) is its 64-bit extension and runs most PCs and servers. It is little-endian.
example: A typical desktop PC runs x86-64 code.

definition: A family of RISC instruction set architectures designed by Arm Ltd, used in almost all phones and in Apple's Mac processors. ARM chips can be configured for either byte order but run little-endian in practice.
example: An iPhone's processor implements the 64-bit ARM architecture.

definition: The 64-bit execution state of the ARM architecture, introduced with ARMv8. It handles most ordinary misaligned loads and stores in hardware but requires alignment for exclusive and atomic instructions.
example: Apple M-series Macs run AArch64 code.

definition: A 32-bit number identifying a device on an IPv4 network, usually written as four decimal octets separated by dots.
example: 192.168.1.10 is 0xC0A8010A as one 32-bit number.

definition: A 16-bit number (0 to 65,535) that identifies which program on a machine a TCP or UDP connection is for.
example: Web servers usually listen on port 443 for HTTPS.

definition: A value holding a memory address, used to refer to data stored elsewhere. On a 64-bit system pointers are normally 64 bits wide.
example: In C, &x gives a pointer to the variable x.

definition: C's basic integer type. Its size is set by the platform; on all mainstream 32- and 64-bit systems it is 32 bits, holding −2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647. unsigned int is the same width with no negative values.
example: On x86-64 Linux, sizeof(int) is 4.

definition: A C integer type of at least 64 bits; in practice exactly 64 bits on mainstream platforms.

C types from <stdint.h> whose width is in the name: int8_t is exactly 8 bits signed, uint32_t exactly 32 bits unsigned, and so on. uintptr_t is an unsigned integer wide enough to hold a pointer. They make sizes explicit when exact layout matters.
example: A network protocol's 32-bit length field is best read into a uint32_t.

definition: The unsigned C type used for sizes and array indices; 64 bits on common 64-bit platforms. Because it is unsigned it can never be negative, so a loop test such as i >= 0 is always true.
example: sizeof returns a size_t.

definition: A popular high-level programming language. Its int type has arbitrary precision, and its float is IEEE 754 binary64.
example: In Python, 2**100 is exact.

aliases: American Standard Code for Information Interchange
definition: The American Standard Code for Information Interchange (1963): a 7-bit character set of 128 codes covering control codes, digits, punctuation and English letters. The first 128 Unicode code points are identical to it.
example: 'A' is 65 (0x41) in ASCII.

definition: An integer type with no sign, so all its bit patterns are zero or positive: n bits hold 0 to 2^n − 1. In C its arithmetic is defined to wrap around.
example: An 8-bit unsigned integer holds 0 to 255.

definition: An integer type that can hold negative as well as positive values. Mainstream processors store signed integers in two's complement.
example: A signed 8-bit integer (int8_t) holds −128 to 127.

definition: The standard way computers store signed integers: the top bit has a negative weight (−128 in 8 bits) and every other bit its normal positive weight. Negation is 'invert every bit and add 1', and the same adder circuit serves signed and unsigned numbers.
example: In 8-bit two's complement, 1111 1011 is −128 + 123 = −5.

definition: A signed-number scheme in which a negative number is every bit of the positive one inverted. It has two zeros (all 0s and all 1s) and needs an end-around carry when adding; today it survives mainly in the Internet checksum.
example: In 8-bit ones' complement, −5 is 1111 1010.

definition: A signed-number scheme that uses the top bit as a sign (0 positive, 1 negative) and the remaining bits as the size. It has two zeros and awkward addition, but IEEE 754 floating point uses it for its sign.
example: In 8-bit sign-magnitude, −5 is 1000 0101.

definition: The bit that indicates whether a signed number is negative: the top bit in two's complement, ones' complement, sign-magnitude and IEEE 754 floats. 1 means negative.
example: Flipping bit 31 of a float changes its sign.

definition: In ones' complement addition, a carry out of the top bit is added back in at the bottom to get the right answer.
example: In 8-bit ones' complement, 1111 1110 (−1) + 0000 0010 (2) gives a carry out; adding it back gives 0000 0001 (1).

definition: The extra 1 produced when adding two numbers overflows the top bit position, like the 1 you carry in column addition. For unsigned numbers it means the true sum did not fit.
example: Adding 200 and 100 in 8 bits produces a carry out and leaves 44.

definition: A 16-bit error-detecting value used in the IPv4, TCP and UDP headers, computed as the ones' complement of the ones' complement sum of the data's 16-bit words (RFC 1071).
example: A router recomputes the IPv4 header checksum each time it decrements the TTL.

definition: A 1964 supercomputer from Control Data Corporation, designed by Seymour Cray; it used 60-bit words and ones' complement integers.
example: The CDC 6600 was the world's fastest computer from 1964 to about 1969.

definition: When the true result of an integer calculation does not fit in the type's range. The hardware keeps only the low bits, so the value wraps; in C, signed overflow is undefined behaviour while unsigned arithmetic is defined to wrap.
example: In 8-bit signed arithmetic, 100 + 28 overflows and wraps to −128.

definition: What happens when a fixed-width value goes past its largest value and continues from its smallest, like an odometer rolling over. It is modular arithmetic on the bit pattern.
example: A 32-bit unsigned millisecond counter wraps to 0 after about 49.7 days.

definition: Widening a signed value by filling the new upper bits with copies of its sign bit, which keeps its value unchanged.
example: −3 as 8 bits is 1111 1101; sign-extended to 16 bits it is 1111 1111 1111 1101.

definition: Widening an unsigned value by filling the new upper bits with 0s, which keeps its value unchanged.
example: The byte 0xFD zero-extended to 16 bits is 0x00FD = 253.

definition: Converting a value to a type with more bits, such as an 8-bit integer to 32 bits. It uses sign extension for signed types and zero extension for unsigned ones.
example: Assigning an int8_t to an int32_t is a widening conversion.

definition: x86 instructions that load and widen a value: movsx sign-extends and movzx zero-extends. ARM's sxtb and uxtb do the same for a byte.
example: Loading an int8_t into a 32-bit register uses movsx.

definition: A status bit set by many processors when an addition carries out of the top bit. On x86 it is also set when a subtraction borrows; ARM uses the opposite sense for subtraction (carry set means no borrow). After an addition it signals unsigned overflow.
example: Adding 0xFF + 0x01 in 8 bits gives 0x00 with the carry flag set.

definition: A status bit set when a signed (two's complement) result has the wrong sign: two positives giving a negative, or two negatives giving a positive. It signals signed overflow.
example: 100 + 100 in 8 bits gives 1100 1000 with the overflow flag set.

definition: Single bits a processor sets after an operation to describe its result, such as zero, negative, carry and overflow; later instructions test them to branch.
example: After cmp eax, ebx, x86 sets flags that a following jl or jb reads.

definition: The contract between hardware and software: the instructions, registers, data types and memory model a processor family provides. x86-64, ARM and RISC-V are ISAs.
example: Programs compiled for x86-64 do not run directly on an ARM ISA.

definition: In C and C++, an operation for which the standard places no requirements at all on what happens, such as signed integer overflow or reading out of bounds. Compilers may assume it never happens, so the effects can be surprising and far from the faulty line.
example: GCC may compile x + 1 < x to false, because signed overflow is UB.

definition: Behaviour that the C standard leaves to each compiler and platform, which must choose one and document it. It is safer than undefined behaviour because it is predictable on a given implementation.
example: Right-shifting a negative int is implementation-defined; GCC documents it as arithmetic.

definition: In C, a valid value that the standard does not pin down and that need not be the same each time, such as the contents of struct padding bytes.
example: Two structs with equal members can have different unspecified padding bytes.

definition: The part of a compiler that rewrites a program to run faster or be smaller while keeping its defined behaviour. It may assume undefined behaviour never happens.
example: At -O2 the optimiser can delete an overflow check that relies on signed wrap.

definition: A compiler option choosing how hard to optimise; -O0 means none and -O2 is the common release setting in GCC and Clang.
example: gcc -O2 enables most optimisations that do not trade size for speed.

definition: C constants from <limits.h> for the largest and smallest int values (2,147,483,647 and −2,147,483,648 for 32-bit int) and the largest unsigned int (4,294,967,295). INT_MIN has no positive counterpart.
example: INT_MAX + 1 is undefined, but UINT_MAX + 1u is 0.

definition: Arithmetic that reports whether the result fitted instead of overflowing silently. GCC and Clang provide __builtin_add_overflow; C23 standardises ckd_add, ckd_sub and ckd_mul in <stdckdint.h>.
example: if (ckd_add(&r, a, b)) handle_error(); catches overflow safely.

definition: A GCC and Clang option that defines signed addition, subtraction and multiplication to wrap around in two's complement, instead of being undefined on overflow.
example: With -fwrapv, INT_MAX + 1 evaluates to INT_MIN.

definition: A GCC option that generates traps (a crash with a signal) for signed overflow in addition, subtraction and multiplication.
example: A program built with -ftrapv aborts when INT_MAX + 1 is computed.

definition: A testing tool built into GCC and Clang that adds run-time checks for many kinds of undefined behaviour, such as signed overflow, and reports them as they happen.
example: clang -fsanitize=undefined test.c builds a binary that reports signed overflow.

definition: The x86 signed integer division instruction. It raises a divide-error exception both for division by zero and when the quotient does not fit, as with INT_MIN / −1.
example: On Linux, the exception from INT_MIN / -1 arrives as SIGFPE.

definition: A condition detected by the processor during an instruction, such as division by zero or an invalid memory access, that stops normal execution and passes control to the operating system. The OS usually turns it into a signal that kills the process.
example: Dividing INT_MIN by −1 on x86 raises a divide-error exception.

definition: The Unix signal sent to a process after an arithmetic error such as integer division by zero (the name means 'floating-point exception', for historical reasons). By default it kills the process.
example: int x = INT_MIN / -1; on x86 Linux usually ends with SIGFPE.

definition: A widely used object-oriented programming language that runs on the Java Virtual Machine. Its int is always 32-bit two's complement and overflow is defined to wrap.
example: In Java, Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1 equals Integer.MIN_VALUE.

definition: Java constants for the smallest and largest int: −2,147,483,648 and 2,147,483,647.
example: Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE) returns Integer.MIN_VALUE.

definition: Java's absolute-value method. For int it returns its argument unchanged when given Integer.MIN_VALUE, because the positive value does not fit.
example: Math.abs(-5) is 5, but Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE) is still negative.

definition: A Java method giving the remainder rounded with floor division, so for a positive divisor the result is never negative.
example: Math.floorMod(-8, 10) is 2, while -8 % 10 is −8.

definition: The Java method that returns an object's 32-bit int hash value, used by HashMap to choose a bucket. It can be any int, including negative ones and Integer.MIN_VALUE.
example: "Aa".hashCode() and "BB".hashCode() are both 2112.

definition: The Java exception thrown when code reads or writes an array with an index below 0 or not less than its length.
example: Indexing a 10-element array with −8 throws it.

definition: One of several partitions that a data set or workload is split across, each held by a different server or table. A hash of the key usually picks the shard.
example: A service with 10 shards might send key k to shard hash(k) mod 10.

definition: C's rules for converting the two operands of an arithmetic or comparison operator to a common type. With int and unsigned int, the int is converted to unsigned, so −1 becomes a huge positive number.
example: -1 < 1u is false in C because −1 becomes 4,294,967,295.

definition: C's rule that small integer types such as char, short and uint8_t are converted to int (or unsigned int) before arithmetic. A uint8_t shifted left is therefore a signed int shift.
example: (uint8_t)0xFF << 24 is computed as an int shift and overflows.

definition: C's ordering of integer types by size (char < short < int < long < long long), used by the usual arithmetic conversions to decide the common type.
example: int and unsigned int have the same rank, so the unsigned one wins.

definition: Command-line options that ask GCC or Clang to warn about suspicious code. -Wall and -Wextra turn on common groups; -Wsign-compare flags signed/unsigned comparisons, -Wtype-limits always-true tests, -Wparentheses precedence traps, -Wpadded padding and -Waddress-of-packed-member pointers to packed fields.
example: gcc -Wall -Wextra warns about if (x & 1 == 0).

definition: An integer type that grows to as many bits as its value needs, limited only by memory, so it never wraps. Python's int and JavaScript's BigInt work this way.
The standard Python library for fast numerical arrays. Its integer types such as np.int8 have fixed widths, so unlike Python's int they wrap on overflow.
example: np.int8(100) + np.int8(100) gives −56.

definition: The first Ariane 5 rocket launch (4 June 1996), destroyed about 37 seconds after lift-off when software reused from Ariane 4 raised an unhandled exception converting a 64-bit floating-point value to a 16-bit signed integer.
example: The inquiry board blamed reused assumptions and inadequate testing, not just one overflow.

definition: A navigation unit that uses gyroscopes and accelerometers to work out a vehicle's position, speed and attitude without outside signals.
example: Ariane 5 carried two identical inertial reference systems, and both failed the same way.

definition: A long-range passenger jet (the Dreamliner). In 2015 the FAA ordered it to be power-cycled periodically because a counter in its generator control units would overflow after 248 days of continuous power.
example: Airlines had to reboot 787 generator control units before 248 days.

definition: The Federal Aviation Administration, the United States regulator for civil aviation; it issues airworthiness directives that operators must follow.
example: The FAA's 2015 directive addressed the 787's 248-day counter overflow.

definition: An aircraft computer that regulates and protects an electrical generator. If all of them shut down at once the aircraft can lose AC electrical power.
example: On the 787, the four main generator control units (those for the engine-mounted generators) could all enter failsafe mode at the same time after 248 days of continuous power.

definition: Electrical current that reverses direction many times a second, the form produced by generators and used for an aircraft's main electrical power.
example: Aircraft AC systems commonly run at 400 Hz.

definition: The failure of software that stores time as a signed 32-bit count of seconds since 1 January 1970: the count runs out at 03:14:07 UTC on 19 January 2038.
example: A signed 32-bit time_t reaches 2,147,483,647 on 19 January 2038.

definition: The C type that holds a calendar time, on Unix systems a count of seconds since 1 January 1970 00:00 UTC (the Unix epoch). It is 64 bits on modern 64-bit systems.
example: time(NULL) returned about 1.7 billion in 2024.

definition: Coordinated Universal Time, the world's reference time standard, which does not change with time zones or daylight saving.
example: The year 2038 limit falls at 03:14:07 UTC.

definition: The low-level rules that compiled code on a platform must follow so separately compiled pieces work together: type sizes and alignments, struct layout, how arguments are passed and so on.
example: The x86-64 System V ABI says long is 8 bytes; the Windows x64 ABI says 4.

definition: One hundredth of a second (10 milliseconds).
example: 2^31 centiseconds is about 248.6 days.

definition: A Windows API function that returns the milliseconds since the system started as an unsigned 32-bit value, so it wraps to 0 after about 49.7 days. GetTickCount64 avoids this.
example: Code comparing GetTickCount values with > breaks at the wrap.

definition: One thousandth of a second.
example: 86,400,000 ms make one day.

definition: An operation that treats an integer as a row of independent bits and works on every position at once, with no carries between positions: AND, OR, XOR, NOT and the shifts.
The bitwise operation (written & in C and Python) whose result bit is 1 only where both input bits are 1. AND with a mask keeps the masked bits and clears the rest.
example: 0xCA & 0x0F is 0x0A.

definition: The bitwise operation (written | in C and Python) whose result bit is 1 where either input bit is 1. OR with a mask sets the masked bits.
example: 0x2C | 0x01 is 0x2D.

definition: The bitwise operation (written ^ in C and Python, ⊕ in maths) whose result bit is 1 where the two input bits differ. XOR with a mask flips the masked bits, and XOR-ing the same value twice undoes it.
The bitwise operation (written ~ in C and Python) that inverts every bit. For two's complement integers, ~x equals −x − 1.
example: ~5 is −6 in Python.

definition: An operator such as && and || in C (and, or in Python) that treats each whole operand as true or false, unlike bitwise operators that work on each bit.
example: 2 && 1 is 1 (true), but 2 & 1 is 0.

definition: Stopping the evaluation of a logical expression as soon as its result is known: in a && b, b is not evaluated when a is false.
example: p && p->x never reads p->x when p is null.

definition: A constant whose 1 bits pick out the positions an operation should affect: AND keeps them, OR sets them, XOR flips them.
example: 0xFF is the mask for the low byte: x & 0xFF keeps only bits 0 to 7.

definition: A single bit used as a yes/no setting. Several flags are packed into one integer and combined with OR, then tested with AND.
example: O_WRONLY | O_CREAT combines two open() flags.

definition: To set a bit is to make it 1 (OR with a mask), to clear it is to make it 0 (AND with the inverted mask), to toggle it is to flip it (XOR with the mask). A 'set bit' is a bit whose value is 1.
example: x |= 1u << 3 sets bit 3; x &= ~(1u << 3) clears it.

definition: The Portable Operating System Interface: IEEE standards for the system calls, commands and C library functions that Unix-like operating systems such as Linux and macOS provide.
example: open(), read() and write() are POSIX functions.

definition: Constants passed to the POSIX open() call. O_CREAT, O_APPEND and similar are single-bit flags combined with OR; the access modes O_RDONLY, O_WRONLY and O_RDWR are alternatives extracted with the O_ACCMODE mask, and O_RDONLY is commonly 0.
example: (flags & O_ACCMODE) == O_WRONLY tests for write-only mode.

definition: A Python enumeration class whose members are bit flags that can be combined with |. The re module's flags such as re.IGNORECASE work the same way.
example: re.IGNORECASE | re.MULTILINE combines two regex options.

definition: A group of adjacent bits inside a larger integer that holds one small value. It is read by shifting down and masking, and written by masking and OR-ing. C also has a struct syntax for bit-fields.
example: Bits 4 to 9 of a register can hold a 6-bit channel number.

definition: A colour stored as red, green and blue intensities, commonly one byte each, written in hex as RRGGBB.
example: #1E90FF is red 30, green 144, blue 255.

definition: The bit layout of a machine instruction: fields for the operation, registers and constants packed into one or more words.
example: A standard (uncompressed) RISC-V instruction is 32 bits, with the opcode in the low 7 bits.

definition: The block of fields at the start of every IPv4 packet: version, length, TTL, protocol, checksum, addresses and so on, several of them packed into bit fields and all multi-byte fields in big-endian order.
example: The first byte of an IPv4 header holds the 4-bit version and 4-bit header length.

definition: A 128-bit identifier designed to be unique without central coordination, written as 32 hex digits in five groups; some of its bits encode its version and variant.
Moving every bit a number of places towards the most significant end and filling with 0s; written <<. Shifting left by k places multiplies by 2 to the power k, as long as no 1 bits are lost.
Moving every bit a number of places towards the least significant end, discarding the low bits; written >>. What fills the top depends on whether it is a logical or an arithmetic shift.
A right shift that fills the vacated top bits with 0s, used for unsigned values. It divides by a power of two, rounding down.
example: 1111 0000 logically shifted right by 2 is 0011 1100.

definition: A right shift that fills the vacated top bits with copies of the sign bit, preserving the sign of a two's complement number. It divides by a power of two rounding towards negative infinity.
example: −16 (1111 0000) arithmetically shifted right by 2 is −4 (1111 1100).

definition: Rounding to the next whole number below, whatever the sign: 2.5 becomes 2 and −2.5 becomes −3. It is the same as the floor function.
example: −17 >> 1 rounds −8.5 towards negative infinity, giving −9.

definition: The rules deciding which operators in an expression are applied first when there are no brackets. In C, & ^ | bind more loosely than ==; in Python they bind more tightly than comparisons.
example: In C, x & 1 == 0 means x & (1 == 0).

definition: The number of 1 bits in a value. x86 has a POPCNT instruction; GCC and Clang offer __builtin_popcount, C23 stdc_count_ones, and Python int.bit_count().
example: popcount(0xF0F0) is 8.

definition: Counting 1 bits by repeatedly doing x &= x − 1, which clears the lowest set bit, until x is 0. The loop runs once per 1 bit rather than once per bit position.
example: For 0b101100 it loops three times.

definition: The number of 0 bits below the lowest 1 bit, which is the position of the lowest set bit. GCC's __builtin_ctz computes it but is undefined for 0.
example: __builtin_ctz(0x2C) is 2, since 0x2C is 101100.

definition: A data structure for running totals over an array that supports updates and prefix sums in O(log n) time. Each node covers a range whose size is the lowest set bit of its index, i & −i.
example: Node 12 (1100) covers 4 elements, because 12 & −12 = 4.

definition: An operation is commutative when order does not matter (a ⊕ b = b ⊕ a) and associative when grouping does not matter ((a ⊕ b) ⊕ c = a ⊕ (b ⊕ c)). XOR is both; floating-point addition is commutative but not associative.
example: (0.1 + 0.2) + 0.3 differs from 0.1 + (0.2 + 0.3) in floats.

definition: Whether the number of 1 bits in a value is odd or even. XOR-ing all the bits gives 1 for odd parity; parity bits are used to detect single-bit errors.
example: 1011 has three 1s, so its parity is odd.

definition: A way of spreading data over several disks with one block of XOR parity per stripe, so the contents of any one failed disk can be rebuilt by XOR-ing the others.
example: With four disks, RAID 5 gives three disks' worth of capacity.

definition: An encryption method that XORs a message with a truly random key as long as the message, used only once. Used correctly it cannot be broken, but the key is impractical to share.
example: Reusing a one-time pad lets an attacker XOR two ciphertexts and cancel the key.

definition: A cipher that turns a short secret key into a long pseudo-random keystream and XORs it with the plaintext.
example: ChaCha20 is the stream cipher used in many TLS connections.

definition: A widely used stream cipher designed by Daniel J. Bernstein, specified for internet protocols in RFC 8439 and used in TLS and WireGuard.
example: ChaCha20 generates its keystream 64 bytes at a time.

definition: In cryptography, plaintext is the readable data before encryption and ciphertext the scrambled result.
example: A stream cipher XORs plaintext with keystream to make ciphertext.

definition: Swapping two variables with three XORs and no temporary (a ^= b; b ^= a; a ^= b). It is a curiosity: it is not faster in practice and zeroes the value if both names refer to the same location.
example: With a = 5 and b = 3, three XORs leave a = 3, b = 5.

definition: When two names or pointers refer to the same memory location, so writing through one changes what the other sees.
example: If a and b alias, the XOR swap sets the value to 0.

definition: A 32-bit IPv4 mask whose 1s mark the network part of an address. AND-ing an address with it gives the network the address belongs to.
example: A /24 network has mask 255.255.255.0 = 0xFFFFFF00.

definition: Classless Inter-Domain Routing notation: /24 after an address means its first 24 bits are the network part, giving the subnet mask with 24 leading 1s.
How IP routers choose a route: among all table entries matching the destination address, use the one with the longest network prefix.
example: A /24 route beats a /16 route for an address both cover.

definition: A 64-bit integer with one bit per square of a chessboard, used by chess engines to compute moves and attacks with shifts and masks.
example: The white pawns at the start are 0x000000000000FF00.

definition: A program that plays or analyses chess. Stockfish, a leading open-source engine, uses bitboards.
example: Stockfish evaluates tens of millions of positions per second on a desktop PC.

definition: A database index that stores one bit per row for each value or condition, so combined conditions are answered by AND-ing or OR-ing the bitmaps.
example: WHERE a AND b becomes bitmap_a & bitmap_b.

definition: A compressed bitmap format that splits the bit range into chunks and stores each as an array, a bitmap or runs, whichever is smallest. Lucene, Druid, Spark and others use it.
example: A sparse set of row IDs takes far less space as a Roaring bitmap.

definition: An open-source Java search library that builds inverted indexes for full-text search; Elasticsearch and Solr are built on it.
example: Elasticsearch stores each shard as a Lucene index.

definition: An open-source analytics database for fast queries over large event data, using compressed bitmap indexes.
example: Druid filters billions of rows using Roaring bitmaps.

definition: Java's standard hash table. It keeps its bucket count a power of two, picks a bucket with hash & (n − 1), and first XORs the hash's top 16 bits into its bottom 16.
example: A new HashMap starts with 16 buckets.

definition: A way of describing how the work or memory an algorithm needs grows with input size n, ignoring constant factors. O(1) means a fixed amount whatever n is; O(n) means growing in proportion to n.
example: Scanning a list once is O(n).

definition: Operating-system code that controls a particular piece of hardware, often by reading and writing bit fields in device registers.
example: A network card's driver sets bits in its control register to start a transfer.

definition: The layers of operating-system code that implement networking protocols such as Ethernet, IP and TCP.
example: Linux's network stack parses IPv4 headers with shifts and masks.

definition: Updating part of a value by reading it, changing some bits and writing it back. On hardware registers the read or write can itself have side effects, and with threads the sequence must be atomic.
example: reg = (reg & ~mask) | value is a read-modify-write.

definition: A way of storing real numbers as a sign, a significand and an exponent, like scientific notation in binary, so one fixed-size format covers both huge and tiny values at a fixed relative precision.
example: A 32-bit float can hold both 3.4 × 10^38 and 1.2 × 10^−38.

definition: The technical standard for floating-point arithmetic, first published in 1985 and revised in 2008 and 2019. It defines the binary16/32/64 formats, rounding, infinities, NaN and subnormals that almost every processor implements.
example: Python's float and C's double are IEEE 754 binary64 on mainstream platforms.

aliases: Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers
definition: The Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, a professional body that publishes engineering standards such as IEEE 754 (floating point) and IEEE 802.11 (Wi-Fi).
example: POSIX is published as IEEE Std 1003.1.

definition: IEC 60559 is the international standard identical to IEEE 754. Annex F of the C standard describes how C maps onto it; a C implementation that follows Annex F guarantees IEEE behaviour such as 1.0 / 0.0 giving infinity.
example: A compiler defining __STDC_IEC_559__ claims Annex F conformance.

definition: The IEEE 754 32-bit format and C's usual float: 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits (bias 127) and 23 fraction bits, giving 24 significant bits, about 7 decimal digits.
example: 0.1 as a float is 0x3DCCCCCD.

definition: The IEEE 754 64-bit format, C's double and Python's float: 1 sign bit, 11 exponent bits (bias 1023) and 52 fraction bits, giving 53 significant bits, about 15 to 16 decimal digits.
The IEEE 754 16-bit format: 1 sign bit, 5 exponent bits (bias 15) and 10 fraction bits. Its largest finite value is only 65,504.
example: 70,000 overflows to infinity in FP16.

definition: A 16-bit floating-point format from Google Brain: 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits and 7 fraction bits. It keeps float32's exponent range (maximum about 3.39 × 10^38) but has only 8 significant bits.
example: Converting float32 to bfloat16 is roughly keeping its top 16 bits, with rounding.

definition: Very small floating-point formats (8 or 4 bits) supported by recent GPUs and accelerators for machine-learning work, trading accuracy for speed and memory.
example: FP8 E4M3 has 4 exponent bits and 3 fraction bits.

definition: An IEEE 754 format with an exactly specified bit layout, such as binary32 or binary64, so values can be exchanged between systems bit for bit.
example: A binary64 value written by one machine reads back identically on another (after any byte-order conversion).

definition: The part of a floating-point number holding its significant digits, the 1.f in (−1)^s × 1.f × 2^E. Older texts call it the mantissa.
example: In 6.02 × 10^3 the significand is 6.02.

definition: The power that the base is raised to. In a floating-point number it sets where the binary point goes; the exponent field stores it with a bias added.
example: In 1.1001 × 2^2 the exponent is 2.

definition: The fixed number added to the true exponent before it is stored, so the exponent field is always an unsigned number: 127 for float, 1023 for double, 15 for half. For a k-bit exponent field it is 2^(k−1) − 1.
example: A true exponent of −3 is stored in a float as −3 + 127 = 124.

definition: A floating-point value written with exactly one non-zero digit before the point, which in binary is always 1. Normal values use exponent fields from 1 to the maximum minus 1 and have the hidden bit.
example: 6.25 normalised is 1.1001 × 2^2.

definition: The leading 1 of a normal binary floating-point significand. Because it is always 1 it is not stored, which gives one extra bit of precision.
example: A float stores 23 fraction bits but has 24 significant bits thanks to the hidden bit.

definition: The stored bits after the binary point of a floating-point significand: 23 in a float, 52 in a double.
example: For 1.1001 × 2^2 the fraction field starts 1001 and is padded with zeros.

term: Round to nearest, ties to even
aliases: round to nearest, ties to even
definition: IEEE 754's default rounding: pick the nearest representable value, and when exactly halfway between two, pick the one whose last bit is 0 (even). This avoids a steady upward bias.
example: Python's round(2.5) is 2 and round(3.5) is 4.

definition: The rule a floating-point unit uses to round results that cannot be represented exactly. IEEE 754 defines round to nearest (the default) and directed modes towards zero, towards +infinity and towards −infinity.
example: In round-towards-zero mode, an overflowing result becomes the largest finite value instead of infinity.

definition: The gap between 1.0 and the next larger representable floating-point number: 2^−23 ≈ 1.19 × 10^−7 for float and 2^−52 ≈ 2.22 × 10^−16 for double. It measures the format's relative precision.
example: 1.0 + 1e-17 == 1.0 in double, because 1e-17 is far below half of epsilon.

definition: The range of floating-point values from one power of two up to (but not including) the next. Within a binade the gap between neighbouring values is constant, and it doubles in the next binade up.
example: All floats from 1.0 to just below 2.0 form one binade, spaced 2^−23 apart.

definition: The size of a number without its sign, written |x|: |−3| = 3 and |3| = 3.

A special floating-point value meaning an undefined result, such as 0/0 or infinity minus infinity. It has an all-ones exponent and a non-zero fraction, spreads through most later arithmetic, and compares unequal to everything, including itself.
example: x != x is true only when x is NaN.

definition: Special IEEE 754 values for results too large to represent, encoded with an all-ones exponent and zero fraction. They come from overflow or non-trapping division by zero and behave sensibly: infinity + 1 is still infinity.
example: 1e308 * 10 is inf in Python.

definition: IEEE 754 has two zeros, +0 (all bits 0) and −0 (only the sign bit set). They compare equal, but keep track of which side a tiny result came from, so 1/−0 is −infinity.
example: 0.0 == -0.0 is True in Python.

definition: A floating-point value with an all-zeros exponent field and non-zero fraction: the hidden bit becomes 0, so values continue in equal steps below the smallest normal number down to zero (for float, as small as 2^−149 ≈ 1.4 × 10^−45).
example: The smallest positive float, 0x00000001, is a subnormal.

definition: When a floating-point result is too close to zero to be a normal number. With gradual underflow it becomes a subnormal; otherwise it is flushed to zero.
example: In float, 1e-30 * 1e-30 underflows to 0.

definition: Processor modes that speed up code by treating subnormals as zero: flush-to-zero (FTZ) replaces subnormal results with 0, and denormals-are-zero (DAZ) treats subnormal inputs as 0. Both change results, so they break strict IEEE behaviour.
example: Audio and game code often enable FTZ and DAZ on x86.

definition: In IEEE 754, an exceptional event such as overflow or division by zero normally just sets a status flag and returns a default result (non-trapping). Trapping arithmetic instead stops the program or calls a handler.
example: Non-trapping 1.0 / 0.0 returns +infinity and sets the divide-by-zero flag.

definition: The Python exception raised for division or modulo by zero, including float division such as 1.0 / 0.0, where IEEE 754 itself would return infinity.
example: 1 / 0.0 raises ZeroDivisionError in Python.

definition: On 25 February 1991 in Dhahran, Saudi Arabia, a Patriot air-defence battery failed to intercept an Iraqi Scud missile, which killed 28 American soldiers. The GAO traced it to a time-conversion precision error that grew to about 0.34 seconds after 100 hours of operation.
example: After 100 hours the system looked in the wrong place for the incoming Scud.

definition: The US Government Accountability Office (called the General Accounting Office until 2004), which audits and investigates for the US Congress.
example: GAO report IMTEC-92-26 analysed the Patriot failure.

definition: A way of adding many floating-point numbers that keeps a separate running correction for the rounding error lost at each step, giving a much more accurate total. Python's math.fsum and (since 3.12) sum() use such techniques.
example: sum([0.1] * 10) is 1.0 in Python 3.12, while a += loop gives 0.9999999999999999.

definition: How far apart two approximate values may be and still count as equal. A relative tolerance scales with the size of the values; an absolute tolerance is a fixed amount, needed near zero. Python's math.isclose takes both.
example: math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3) is True with its default relative tolerance of 1e-9.

definition: A number type that stores base-10 digits exactly, so values like 0.10 have no binary rounding error. Python has decimal.Decimal and SQL has NUMERIC (also called DECIMAL). It is the usual choice for money.
example: Decimal('0.10') * 10 == Decimal('1.00') is True.

definition: The smallest unit of a currency, such as pence or cents. Storing money as a whole number of minor units avoids floating-point rounding.
example: £12.34 is stored as the integer 1234 pence.

definition: The large relative error that appears when two nearly equal approximate numbers are subtracted: the matching leading digits cancel and mostly rounding error is left.
example: Computing 1 − cos(x) for tiny x directly loses most of its digits.

definition: How sensitive a calculation's result is to small errors in its inputs. A badly conditioned problem amplifies input errors however carefully it is computed.
example: Solving a nearly singular system of equations is ill-conditioned.

definition: Combining many values into one (such as a sum) by splitting the work across many threads and merging partial results. Because float addition is not associative, the merge order can change the last bits of the answer.
example: A GPU sum of a million floats may differ slightly between runs.

definition: A machine-learning model built from layers of simple units connected by learned numeric weights, trained by repeatedly adjusting the weights to reduce errors.
example: Large language models are neural networks with billions of weights.

definition: In machine learning, a multi-dimensional array of numbers, such as a matrix of weights or a batch of images.
example: A batch of 32 RGB images of 224 × 224 pixels is a 32 × 3 × 224 × 224 tensor.

definition: The output value of a unit or layer in a neural network, computed during the forward pass and passed to the next layer.
example: Activations above 65,504 overflow in FP16.

definition: In training, the set of values saying how much a small change in each weight would change the error; weights are moved against it. Gradients are often very small numbers.
example: A gradient of 1e-8 underflows to 0 in FP16.

definition: A mixed-precision training technique that multiplies the loss by a large factor so small gradients stay representable in FP16, then divides the factor back out before updating weights.
example: Scaling the loss by 1,024 lifts a 1e-8 gradient into FP16's range.

definition: A variable or register that sums many values. In reduced-precision computing, sums are often kept in a wider format (such as float32) to limit rounding error.
example: Tensor cores multiply FP16 values but can accumulate in float32.

definition: Google's custom chip for machine-learning workloads, which popularised the bfloat16 format.
example: Google Cloud TPUs perform matrix multiplication in bfloat16.

definition: JavaScript's arbitrary-precision integer type, written with an n suffix (123n), for integers beyond the exact range of ordinary Number values.
example: 2n ** 64n is exact as a BigInt.

definition: The largest integer n such that n and n + 1 are both exactly representable as a JavaScript Number (a binary64 double): 2^53 − 1 = 9,007,199,254,740,991.
example: Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER + 2 evaluates to 9,007,199,254,740,992.

definition: The programming language of web browsers, also used on servers (Node.js). Its ordinary numbers are all IEEE 754 doubles, and its strings are sequences of UTF-16 code units.
Python's module for converting between values and packed bytes using a format string; a prefix character chooses byte order and alignment (@ native, < little-endian, > big-endian, ! network).
example: struct.pack('>f', -6.25).hex() gives 'c0c80000'.

definition: An agreed list of characters with a number assigned to each. In Unicode the number is called a code point. The word charset is also used loosely to mean an encoding.
example: In ASCII, the character set gives 'A' the number 65.

definition: The rule that turns a character set's numbers into bytes and back. UTF-8, UTF-16 and Windows-1252 are encodings; reading bytes with the wrong one garbles text.
example: 'é' is the bytes C3 A9 in UTF-8 but the single byte E9 in Latin-1.

definition: The number Unicode assigns to a character or other encoded element, written U+ followed by at least four hex digits. The code space runs from U+0000 to U+10FFFF.
example: € is code point U+20AC.

definition: The universal character standard that gives every character in the world's writing systems, plus symbols and emoji, a unique code point. Its first 128 code points match ASCII.
example: Unicode 15.0 encodes about 149,000 characters.

definition: Any Unicode code point except the surrogates (U+D800 to U+DFFF): the values that UTF-8, UTF-16 and UTF-32 can encode. There are 1,112,064 of them.
example: U+1F600 is a scalar value; U+D83D is not.

definition: The dominant Unicode encoding: 1 to 4 bytes per code point, with ASCII unchanged as single bytes. Lead bytes start 0, 110, 1110 or 11110 and continuation bytes start 10. Defined in RFC 3629.
example: € (U+20AC) is E2 82 AC in UTF-8.

definition: A Unicode encoding using 16-bit code units: one unit for code points up to U+FFFF (except surrogates) and a surrogate pair of two units above that. Its byte order is little-endian (LE) or big-endian (BE). Java, JavaScript and Windows strings use it.
example: 😀 is D83D DE00 in UTF-16.

definition: A Unicode encoding that stores every scalar value as one 32-bit code unit: simple to index but four bytes per character, with a byte order to choose.
example: 'A' is 00 00 00 41 in UTF-32BE.

definition: An obsolete fixed-width 16-bit Unicode encoding that could only represent the Basic Multilingual Plane. UTF-16 extended it with surrogate pairs.
example: Windows NT originally used UCS-2 before moving to UTF-16.

definition: The fixed-size unit an encoding works in: 8 bits in UTF-8, 16 in UTF-16, 32 in UTF-32. One code point takes one or more code units.
example: 😀 is two UTF-16 code units.

definition: The character U+FEFF placed at the start of a text file to show its encoding and byte order: FF FE means UTF-16 little-endian, FE FF big-endian, and EF BB BF marks UTF-8.
example: A UTF-16LE file usually starts with the bytes FF FE.

definition: A character code that means an action rather than a printable symbol, such as newline (10) or tab (9). ASCII codes 0 to 31 and 127 are control codes (the C0 set); 128 to 159 are the C1 set.
example: Code 10 is the line feed control code.

definition: A legacy 8-bit encoding that keeps ASCII in codes 0 to 127 and uses 128 to 255 for one region's extra characters. Many incompatible code pages exist.
example: Windows code page 1252 is Western European; 1251 is Cyrillic.

definition: An 8-bit character set for Western European languages; its 256 codes are identical to the first 256 Unicode code points.
example: é is the single byte E9 in Latin-1.

definition: Microsoft's Western European code page. It matches Latin-1 except that most of 0x80 to 0x9F hold printable characters such as € and curly quotes instead of C1 controls. UTF-8 decoded as Windows-1252 produces typical mojibake.
example: The UTF-8 bytes E2 80 99 read as Windows-1252 give â€™.

definition: An 8-bit code page for Russian Cyrillic text, common on Unix systems before Unicode.
example: Opening a KOI8-R file as Windows-1252 shows gibberish Latin letters.

definition: A variable-width encoding for Japanese using one or two bytes per character, based on the JIS (Japanese Industrial Standards) character sets.
example: Older Japanese websites were often in Shift JIS.

definition: Garbled text produced when bytes are decoded with a different encoding from the one used to write them; the Japanese word means roughly 'character transformation'.
example: café shown as cafÃ© is mojibake from UTF-8 read as Windows-1252.

definition: One of 17 blocks of 65,536 code points in the Unicode code space, numbered 0 to 16. Plane 0 is the Basic Multilingual Plane; planes 1 to 16 are supplementary and need 4 bytes in UTF-8 and a surrogate pair in UTF-16.
example: 😀 (U+1F600) is in plane 1.

definition: Unicode plane 0, code points U+0000 to U+FFFF, holding most characters of modern scripts. BMP characters (except surrogates) take one UTF-16 code unit.
example: € (U+20AC) is in the BMP; 😀 is not.

definition: Chinese, Japanese and Korean characters. Unicode unifies the shared Han ideographs (symbols for words or ideas) into the CJK Unified Ideographs blocks, mostly in the BMP and plane 2.
example: 你 (U+4F60) is a CJK unified ideograph.

definition: Picture characters encoded in Unicode, mostly in plane 1 (so they need 4 UTF-8 bytes), though some are in the BMP. Many are sequences of several code points.
example: 😀 is U+1F600 GRINNING FACE.

definition: Unicode code point ranges that will never be assigned standard characters, left for organisations to use privately, for example for custom icons.
example: U+E000 to U+F8FF is the BMP private-use area.

definition: One of 66 Unicode code points permanently reserved for internal use, such as U+FFFE and U+FFFF; they should not appear in interchanged text.
example: U+FFFE is a noncharacter, which is why a byte-swapped BOM is easy to detect.

definition: Two UTF-16 code units, a high surrogate (D800 to DBFF) then a low surrogate (DC00 to DFFF), that together encode one code point above U+FFFF. The range D800 to DFFF is reserved for this and holds no characters.
example: 😀 (U+1F600) is the surrogate pair D83D DE00.

definition: The first unit of a UTF-16 surrogate pair, in the range D800 to DBFF; it carries the top 10 bits of the code point minus 0x10000.
example: D83D is the high surrogate for 😀 and 👍.

definition: The second unit of a UTF-16 surrogate pair, in the range DC00 to DFFF; it carries the low 10 bits of the code point minus 0x10000.
example: DE00 is the low surrogate for 😀.

definition: A high or low surrogate without its partner, usually from cutting a UTF-16 string in the middle of a pair. JavaScript strings can hold one, but it is not valid UTF-16 or UTF-8 text.
example: '😀'.slice(0, 1) in JavaScript is a lone surrogate.

definition: The first byte of a multi-byte UTF-8 sequence. Its leading 1 bits (110, 1110 or 11110) give the total length of the sequence.
example: E2 (1110 0010) is the lead byte of a 3-byte sequence.

definition: A byte after the lead byte in a multi-byte UTF-8 sequence; it always starts with the bits 10, so it lies between 0x80 and 0xBF.
example: 82 and AC are the continuation bytes in E2 82 AC.

definition: In UTF-8, the bits of each byte that carry the code point itself, after the marker bits that say what kind of byte it is.
example: A 3-byte UTF-8 sequence has 4 + 6 + 6 = 16 payload bits.

definition: An encoding in which you can find the start of the next character from any position, without reading from the beginning. UTF-8 is one, because continuation bytes always start with 10.
example: Jumping into the middle of a UTF-8 file, skip at most 3 continuation bytes to resync.

definition: A sequence of bytes ending with a zero byte (NUL), the way C represents text. Its length is found by counting to the NUL, and the format says nothing about the encoding.
example: "hi" in C occupies 3 bytes: 68 69 00.

definition: The character with code 0. C uses it to mark the end of a string, so text containing U+0000 cannot be held in an ordinary C string.
example: UTF-8 never produces a 0 byte except for U+0000 itself.

definition: The C function that counts the bytes in a string before its terminating NUL. It counts bytes, not characters.
example: strlen("é") is 2 when the literal is UTF-8 encoded.

definition: Dictionary-style ordering: compare the first elements, and only if they are equal move on to the next. Comparing valid UTF-8 byte strings this way gives code point order.
example: 'abc' sorts before 'abd' because c < d.

definition: Language-aware rules for sorting and comparing text, such as ignoring case or treating accented letters specially; it differs from comparing raw code points.
example: MySQL's utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci collation is accent- and case-insensitive.

definition: The numbered document series published by the IETF that defines internet standards. RFC 3629 defines UTF-8; RFC 8259 defines JSON.
example: RFC 791 defines IPv4.

definition: A systems programming language focused on memory safety; its str type is always valid UTF-8 and str.len() counts bytes.
example: 'é'.len() is 2 in Rust.

definition: A compiled programming language from Google. Go source is UTF-8, and len on a Go string counts bytes, though a string may hold arbitrary bytes.
example: len("é") is 2 in Go.

definition: What a reader sees as one character, which may be several code points, for example a letter plus a combining accent or an emoji with a skin-tone modifier. Unicode's segmentation rules (UAX #29) define the boundaries.
example: 👍🏽 is one grapheme cluster made of two code points.

definition: A code point that modifies the preceding character instead of standing alone, such as U+0301 COMBINING ACUTE ACCENT, which turns e into é.
example: e followed by U+0301 displays as é.

definition: One of five Unicode code points (U+1F3FB to U+1F3FF) that follow a person or hand emoji to change its skin colour; the pair displays as one symbol.
example: 👍 followed by U+1F3FD gives 👍🏽.

definition: 26 Unicode letters (U+1F1E6 to U+1F1FF) used in pairs to spell a country code; the pair is shown as that country's flag.
example: The regional indicators G and B display as 🇬🇧.

definition: The invisible character U+200D, used between emoji to ask for them to be shown as one combined emoji, such as a family.
example: 👨 ZWJ 👩 ZWJ 👧 can display as one family emoji.

definition: The JavaScript API that splits text into grapheme clusters, words or sentences according to Unicode rules.
example: [...new Intl.Segmenter().segment('👍🏽')].length is 1.

definition: A third-party Python regular-expression library, more Unicode-aware than the built-in re; its \X pattern matches one grapheme cluster.
example: regex.findall(r'\X', '👍🏽') returns one item.

definition: Converting text to a standard form so that strings that look identical are also identical in code points. Unicode defines four normal forms: NFC, NFD, NFKC and NFKD (UAX #15).
example: After normalising to NFC, 'e' + U+0301 becomes the single code point U+00E9.

definition: Unicode Normalization Form C (canonical composition): decompose, then recombine into precomposed characters where possible. The usual choice for storing and comparing text.
example: NFC turns e + U+0301 into é (U+00E9).

definition: Unicode Normalization Form D (canonical decomposition): split precomposed characters into base letters plus combining marks.
example: NFD turns é (U+00E9) into e + U+0301.

definition: Unicode Normalization Form KC: like NFC but also replaces compatibility variants, such as ligatures and full-width letters, with their plain equivalents. Useful for search and usernames; NFKD is the decomposed version.
example: NFKC turns the ligature ﬁ into the two letters fi.

definition: Unicode's term for two code point sequences that represent the same character and should look and behave the same, such as é as one code point or as e plus a combining accent.
example: U+00E9 and U+0065 U+0301 are canonically equivalent.

definition: A single code point for a letter with an accent, such as é (U+00E9), as opposed to the decomposed form: a base letter followed by combining marks.
example: café typed on most keyboards uses the precomposed é.

definition: Two or more letters joined into one glyph, such as ﬁ. Unicode has a few compatibility code points for ligatures, which NFKC replaces with the separate letters.
example: ﬁ is U+FB01 LATIN SMALL LIGATURE FI.

definition: Apple's Mac file system from 1998 until APFS (2017); it stored file names in a modified form of Unicode decomposition.
example: On HFS+, a file named café was stored with e + U+0301.

definition: A UTF-8 sequence that uses more bytes than necessary for a code point, such as C0 AF for '/'. RFC 3629 forbids them because they can sneak characters past security checks.
example: Decoders must reject C0 AF rather than turning it into '/'.

definition: An attack that uses ../ sequences in a path to reach files outside the directory a server meant to expose.
example: GET /files/../../etc/passwd is a traversal attempt.

definition: Microsoft's web server for Windows. In 2000 it was hit by a directory traversal attack using an overlong UTF-8 encoding of '/'.
example: The attack used URLs containing ..%c0%af...

definition: Converting data that has several possible spellings into one standard form before checking or comparing it, so a check cannot be bypassed with an alternative spelling.
example: A URL path is canonicalised by decoding it and resolving ../ before access checks.

definition: Uniform Resource Locator: the address of a resource on the web, such as https://example.com/files/a.txt. The part after the host name is the path, which a web server maps to a file or handler.
example: In https://example.com/files/a.txt the path is /files/a.txt.

definition: A widely used open-source relational database. Its character set named utf8 is really utf8mb3 (up to 3 bytes per character); full UTF-8 is utf8mb4, the default since MySQL 8.0.
example: CREATE TABLE t (...) CHARACTER SET utf8mb4; stores emoji.

definition: MySQL character sets: utf8mb4 is true UTF-8 (1 to 4 bytes per character); utf8mb3, historically called utf8, stops at 3 bytes and so cannot store characters above U+FFFF such as many emoji.
example: Inserting 😀 into a utf8mb3 column is rejected in strict SQL mode.

definition: The HTTP header that states a body's media type and, for text, its character encoding, as in text/html; charset=utf-8.
example: Without charset=utf-8, a browser may guess the wrong encoding.

definition: A negative constant (usually −1) that C's character functions use to signal end of file; toupper and similar accept it as well as unsigned char values.
example: getchar() returns EOF when input ends.

definition: C library functions that change the case of a single char according to the current C locale. They work on bytes, not Unicode characters.
example: toupper('a') is 'A'.

definition: The settings that tell a program which language and regional conventions to use, including how to classify characters and format numbers.
example: In the default C locale, toupper only changes ASCII letters.

definition: Python 3's two text-related types: bytes is a sequence of raw byte values, str a sequence of code points. .encode() turns str into bytes and .decode() does the reverse, each using a named encoding.
example: 'é'.encode('utf-8') is b'\xc3\xa9'.

definition: Comma-separated values: a plain-text table format with one record per line. It has no standard way to declare its encoding, so programs often guess.
example: A CSV opened with the wrong encoding shows mojibake.

definition: A number identifying one location in memory. In the byte-addressed model each address names one byte, so a 4-byte integer occupies four consecutive addresses.
example: A uint32_t at address 100 uses addresses 100 to 103.

definition: Memory in which every individual byte has its own address, the model used by almost all modern processors.
example: On a byte-addressed machine, address 101 is the second byte of a word starting at 100.

definition: Storing a multi-byte value with its most significant byte at the lowest address, the order we write numbers in. Network protocols and formats such as PNG use it.
Storing a multi-byte value with its least significant byte at the lowest address. x86 and, in practice, ARM and RISC-V systems use it.
A processor that can be configured to run in either big-endian or little-endian mode. ARM, PowerPC and MIPS are bi-endian.
example: Most ARM systems run their bi-endian cores in little-endian mode.

definition: The order in which the bytes of a multi-byte value are stored or sent: big-endian or little-endian. Another name for endianness.
example: A file format must state its byte order or record it in a header.

definition: Big-endian order, the standard for multi-byte fields in TCP/IP headers. Host byte order is whatever the local machine uses, so programs convert at the boundary.
example: Port 8080 in network byte order is the bytes 1F 90.

definition: C functions that convert between host byte order and network byte order for 32-bit (l, 'long') and 16-bit (s, 'short') values. On big-endian hosts they do nothing.
example: addr.sin_port = htons(8080); stores the port in network order.

definition: An operating-system endpoint for network communication. A server creates a socket, binds it to an address and port, then listens for connections.
example: bind() fails if another process already uses the port.

definition: The C struct holding an IPv4 socket address; its sin_port and sin_addr fields must be in network byte order.
example: sin_port = htons(443) sets port 443.

definition: The internet protocol suite, named after its two main protocols TCP and IP. Its multi-byte header fields are big-endian.
example: A TCP/IP packet carries its port numbers big-endian.

definition: Portable Network Graphics, a lossless image file format whose multi-byte integers are big-endian.
example: A PNG file begins with the 8 bytes 89 50 4E 47 0D 0A 1A 0A.

definition: A common lossy image format (from the Joint Photographic Experts Group); the lengths of its marker segments are big-endian.
example: A JPEG file starts with the marker FF D8.

definition: A compressed archive file format whose header fields are little-endian.
example: Every ZIP local file header starts with 50 4B 03 04 ('PK').

definition: A simple Windows image file format whose header fields are little-endian.
example: A .bmp file starts with the bytes 'BM'.

definition: Tagged Image File Format, which records its byte order in its first two bytes: II for Intel (little-endian) or MM for Motorola (big-endian).
example: A little-endian TIFF starts 49 49 2A 00.

definition: The compiled binary file the Java Virtual Machine loads; its multi-byte items are big-endian.
example: Every class file starts with the magic number CA FE BA BE.

definition: IBM's 64-bit mainframe architecture, a big-endian descendant of System/360.
example: Bank mainframes running z/OS use z/Architecture.

definition: An open, royalty-free instruction set architecture. Common RISC-V systems are little-endian, though the ISA also defines big-endian modes.
example: Many new microcontrollers use RISC-V cores.

definition: A RISC architecture from Apple, IBM and Motorola, used in older Macs and game consoles; it is bi-endian but traditionally big-endian.
example: The Nintendo Wii used a PowerPC processor.

definition: A classic RISC architecture, long used in routers and embedded devices and widely taught; it is bi-endian.
example: Many textbooks teach assembly language using MIPS.

definition: A RISC architecture from Sun Microsystems, big-endian and strict about alignment: misaligned loads trap.
example: Solaris servers traditionally ran on SPARC.

definition: A widely used open-source Unix-like operating system kernel, running most servers and Android phones.
example: 64-bit Linux uses the x86-64 System V ABI on PCs.

definition: Placing a value at an address that is a whole multiple of its own size, such as a 4-byte int at an address divisible by 4.
example: An 8-byte double at address 0x1018 is naturally aligned.

definition: The rule that a value should start at an address that is a multiple of some power of two, its alignment. The ABI sets each type's alignment, usually equal to its size for basic types.
example: A struct containing a double usually has 8-byte alignment.

definition: A memory access to an address that is not a multiple of the value's alignment. It may be slower, may cross a cache line or page, may fault on strict-alignment CPUs, and in C is undefined behaviour.
example: Reading a 4-byte int from address 62 is misaligned.

definition: A processor or mode that does not support some misaligned accesses: it faults or behaves unexpectedly instead of handling them.
example: An Arm Cortex-M0 faults on a misaligned 32-bit load.

definition: The fixed-size block (commonly 64 bytes) in which data moves between main memory and the CPU caches. An access that crosses a line boundary may need two lines.
example: Two counters in the same 64-byte cache line can cause false sharing.

definition: The fixed-size block (commonly 4 KiB) in which the operating system maps virtual addresses to physical memory. An access crossing a page boundary needs two translations.
example: A 4 KiB page spans addresses 0x1000 to 0x1FFF.

definition: Converting a virtual address to a physical address using page tables, usually cached in a TLB.
example: Each load of a new page may need a page-table walk.

definition: An x86 instruction prefix that makes a read-modify-write instruction atomic with respect to other processors.
example: lock add [mem], 1 increments a shared counter atomically.

definition: An x86 atomic (lock-prefixed) operation on data that crosses two cache lines. The CPU must lock the whole bus or equivalent, stalling other cores; recent Linux kernels can detect and warn about or slow down processes that do this.
example: A lock-prefixed add on an int at address 62 is a split lock.

definition: An operation that other threads or processors see as happening all at once, never half done. Hardware usually needs aligned data to guarantee it.
example: An aligned 8-byte store on x86-64 is atomic, so no thread sees half the value.

definition: When another thread sees part of an old value and part of a new one because a memory access was not done as one indivisible operation.
example: A misaligned 8-byte store split across two lines can tear.

definition: In C and C++, two threads accessing the same memory without synchronisation where at least one writes. It is undefined behaviour even if the hardware access cannot tear.
example: Two threads doing counter++ on a plain int is a data race.

definition: ARM's instructions for building atomic updates: a load-exclusive marks an address, and the matching store-exclusive only succeeds if no one else wrote it in between. They require aligned addresses.
example: AArch64 LDXR/STXR implement compare-and-swap loops.

definition: A small computer on one chip with processor, memory and input/output, used in embedded devices. Many cannot perform misaligned accesses.
example: An Arm Cortex-M0 microcontroller faults on misaligned loads.

definition: The Unix signal for a bus error, such as an unsupported misaligned access on some systems or touching a mapped file beyond its end. By default it kills the process.
example: A misaligned load on a strict-alignment CPU can end in SIGBUS.

definition: An asynchronous notification the operating system sends to a process, often to report an error such as SIGSEGV, SIGBUS or SIGFPE; by default most kill the process.
example: Pressing Ctrl-C sends SIGINT.

definition: The C library function that copies a given number of bytes from one memory location to another. Copying into a properly typed local variable is the safe way to read an unaligned or differently typed value.
example: memcpy(&v, buf, 4) reads 4 bytes into v at any alignment.

definition: The C library function that compares two blocks of memory byte by byte. It is unreliable for structs, because padding bytes can differ even when the members are equal.
