example: memcmp(&a, &b, sizeof a) may report unequal structs that have equal fields.

definition: The C library function that fills a block of memory with one byte value, often zero.
example: memset(&s, 0, sizeof s) zeroes a whole struct, padding included.

definition: C library functions that write and read raw bytes to and from a file. Writing a struct with them copies its in-memory layout, padding and byte order included.
example: fwrite(&s, sizeof s, 1, f) writes the struct's exact bytes.

definition: A Linux kernel function that copies bytes from kernel memory to a user program's memory. Copying a struct with uninitialised padding this way can leak kernel data.
example: A driver returns results to user space with copy_to_user.

definition: The memory and privilege level where ordinary programs run, separated from kernel space where the operating system runs. Data crosses between them only through controlled interfaces.
example: A system call switches from user space into the kernel.

definition: A compiler optimisation that turns a loop over single values into SIMD instructions processing several values at once. Vectorisers may assume pointers are correctly aligned.
example: A loop adding two float arrays can be vectorised to add 8 floats per AVX instruction.

definition: In C, the full sequence of bytes that makes up an object in memory, including any padding bytes.
example: The object representation of struct A is 12 bytes, 6 of them padding.

definition: A C type that groups several named members of possibly different types into one object, laid out in declaration order with padding for alignment.
example: struct point { int x; int y; } is 8 bytes.

definition: Unused bytes a compiler inserts between struct members so each member is properly aligned. Their contents are unspecified.
example: struct {char a; int b;} has 3 padding bytes after a.

definition: Padding at the end of a struct so its size is a multiple of its alignment, which keeps every element of an array of the structs aligned.
example: struct {char; int; char} has 3 bytes of tail padding, making it 12 bytes.

definition: A C macro giving the byte offset of a member from the start of its struct; an offset is a distance in bytes from a starting address.
example: offsetof(struct A, c) is 8.

definition: The C operator giving the size in bytes of a type or object, including all padding.
example: sizeof(struct A) is 12 on x86-64.

definition: C and C++ operators to query (_Alignof / alignof) or raise (alignas) the alignment of a type or object.
example: alignas(64) int counter; starts the counter on a 64-byte boundary.

definition: The ABI family used by Linux and most Unix-like systems, defining type sizes, alignment and struct layout for each processor (x86-64, i386 and others).
example: Under the x86-64 System V ABI, double is 8-byte aligned.

definition: Giving a type or object a stricter alignment than its natural one, for example with alignas(64).
example: A cache-line-aligned counter is over-aligned to 64 bytes.

definition: A Linux tool (from the dwarves package) that reads debugging information and prints each struct's layout, showing every hole and padding byte.
example: pahole -C 'struct A' a.out shows the 3-byte holes.

definition: A struct declared without padding, using compiler extensions such as GCC's __attribute__((packed)) or #pragma pack(1), to match an exact file or wire format. Members may be misaligned.
example: A packed struct {char; int; char} is 6 bytes.

definition: Address space layout randomisation: the operating system places code, stack and heap at random addresses so attackers cannot predict them. A leaked pointer defeats it.
example: Each run of a program on Linux gets a different stack address.

definition: Memory that has not been written since it was allocated, so it still holds whatever was there before, possibly secret data.
example: Stack padding bytes may contain an old pointer.

definition: Turning in-memory data into a defined sequence of bytes for a file or network, and back again (deserialisation), independent of padding and byte order.
example: Writing each field big-endian is a simple serialisation.

definition: Serialisation formats with exactly specified byte layouts: Google's Protocol Buffers, FlatBuffers and Cap'n Proto. A schema describes the fields and code is generated to read and write them.
example: A Protocol Buffers message encodes an int field as a varint.

definition: Laying data out with the same sizes and alignment the platform's C compiler would use. Python's struct module does this with the @ prefix.
example: struct.calcsize('@ci') is 8 on x86-64.

definition: Python's standard library for calling C functions and describing C data; ctypes.Structure lays out fields like a C struct on supported ABIs, including padding.
example: ctypes.sizeof of a char-int-char Structure is 12.

definition: x86 SIMD instruction set extensions with 256-bit (AVX, AVX2) and 512-bit (AVX-512) registers. Some of their load forms require aligned addresses; others accept unaligned ones.
example: One AVX instruction adds eight 32-bit floats at once.

definition: A slowdown when threads on different CPU cores update different variables that happen to share a cache line, so the line keeps moving between the cores' caches.
example: Two counters 8 bytes apart, updated by two threads, suffer false sharing.

definition: One independent processing unit inside a CPU chip, with its own registers and usually its own small caches.
example: An 8-core CPU can run 8 threads truly in parallel.

definition: The hardware protocol that keeps every core's cached copy of a memory location consistent, for example by invalidating other copies when one core writes.
example: MESI is a common cache coherence protocol.

definition: A C++17 constant giving the implementation's suggested minimum distance between objects to avoid false sharing; typically 64 on x86-64.
example: alignas(std::hardware_destructive_interference_size) separates two counters.

definition: C and POSIX functions that allocate memory starting at an address with a requested alignment. They do not make memory physically contiguous or ready for DMA.
example: aligned_alloc(4096, 8192) returns page-aligned memory.

definition: Hardware that lets a device such as a disk or network card read and write main memory directly, without the CPU copying each byte.
example: A network card uses DMA to place received packets in memory.

definition: Memory locked in place in physical RAM so the operating system will not move or swap it out, as DMA requires.
example: GPU transfers are faster from pinned host memory.

definition: A tool that runs a program under control so you can pause it, step through it and inspect memory and variables.
example: In GDB, x/4xb &v prints the 4 bytes of v.

definition: Microsoft's software platform and runtime for C# and other languages; its strings are sequences of UTF-16 code units.
example: In C#, "😀".Length is 2.

definition: A cross-platform C++ application framework; its QString class stores text as UTF-16 code units.
example: QString::size() counts UTF-16 code units.

definition: The Windows API functions ending in W (such as CreateFileW) that take strings as UTF-16 code units, alongside older A versions that take code-page bytes.
example: CreateFileW accepts any Unicode file name.

definition: Division of whole numbers that gives a whole-number result. In C (since C99) and Java it truncates towards zero, so −7 / 2 is −3; Python's // instead floors, giving −4. Integer division by zero is undefined behaviour in C.
example: In C, 7 / 2 is 3.

definition: Moving all the bits of a value left or right by a number of places, the shift count. Left shifts multiply by powers of two; right shifts divide. In C, a shift count that is negative or at least the operand's width is undefined behaviour.
example: 0b0001 shifted left by 3 is 0b1000.

definition: The low bits of a value are its least significant positions (the right-hand end); the high bits are its most significant ones (the left-hand end).
example: The low 8 bits of 0x1234 are 0x34.

definition: How many images (frames) a game or video draws each second.
example: At 60 frames a second, a game renders 5,184,000 frames a day.

definition: One transfer between the processor and the memory system, such as reading one cache line. A misaligned access can need two.
example: A load that crosses a 64-byte line boundary needs two memory transactions.

definition: The compiler stage that turns the program into machine instructions; generated code is its output. Options such as -fwrapv change what code it emits.
example: At -O2, the generated code for x + 1 < x may be just return 0.

definition: A file holding raw bytes in a defined layout rather than readable text, such as an image, an executable or a database page.
example: A PNG is a binary file whose integers are big-endian.

definition: Filling with zeros: writing extra leading 0 digits so numbers line up (which in C turns a literal into octal), or filling unused bytes with zero.
example: Writing 7 as 007 is zero padding; in C, 010 means eight.

definition: An opt-in JavaScript mode ('use strict') that turns some legacy behaviours into errors; outside it (non-strict code), legacy octal literals such as 010 are still accepted.
example: In strict mode, 010 is a SyntaxError.
